title: Personal and Social Worries Associated with the Likelihood of Having Children
population: German adults; total sample and childless subsample
exposure_measure_content: Worry about the impact of climate change, 3-point scale (not worried / somewhat worried / very worried), SOEP worry battery item
exposure_items_quoted: (1) protection of the environment ... (6) the impact of climate change ... answered on a 3-point scale
sample_independence_note: SHARES GSOEP WITH peters_2023_soep_reciprocal — the two are NOT independent samples and must not be pooled as if they were
notes: THE LOAD-BEARING REALIZED STUDY, and it does not survive its own robustness check. Model 2 adjusts for education, income, employment, all personality traits, AND political attitudes — the only realized study that beats the D.1.a confound by design. BUT: after additionally adjusting for the summary score of all OTHER worries, only own health, crime in Germany, and immigration remained significant — climate change did NOT. That is a within-study failure of the Wall 2 discrimination the whole hypothesis depends on. Separately, in the childless sample over the full 1984-2020 span the climate association was not significant; the 16% figure is the 2009-2020 window only.

title: Attitudes towards childbearing, population, and the environment: prevalence, correlates, and connections with fertility outcomes in Sweden
authors: Kirsti M. Jylhä; Martin Kolk; Malcolm Fairbrother
exposure_measure_content: Climate change worry; worry about overpopulation; worry about future generations — separate items
exposure_items_quoted: climate change worry / worry about overpopulation / worry about future generations
notes: Largest sample in the realized stratum and a NULL by the authors' own conclusion: 'we see no clear evidence of their impact on childbearing decisions in Sweden'. Sign structure matters and is not one-directional: worry about future generations correlates POSITIVELY with number of children (r=+0.06) and carries a positive regression coefficient (b=+0.12), while overpopulation worry is negative (b=-0.11). Climate-change worry itself is negative but very weak bivariately (r=-0.04).

title: Too Worried about the Environment to Have Children? Or More Worried about the Environment After Having Children? The Reciprocal Relationship Between Environmental Concerns and Fertility
authors: Steffen Peters; Erich Striessnig; Maria Rita Testa; Alessandra Trimarchi; Natalie Nitsche
exposure_measure_content: Yearly SOEP environmental-concern measures over the life course
exposure_items_quoted: yearly measures of environmental concerns (1984 to 2020)
sample_independence_note: SHARES GSOEP WITH golovina_2024_soep_worries — NOT independent
notes: The reverse-causality design the chapter calls the most valuable in the set, and it returns a NULL: no significant relationship between environmental concerns early in or throughout the life course and first birth timing or quantum, except individuals born before 1970 who delayed parenthood. Trajectory differences between eventual parents and the childless are attributed by the authors largely to unobserved heterogeneity. Working paper with limited review per its own cover page.

title: Climate change narratives and first births in the UK
authors: Ewa Weychert; Daniele Vignoli; Anna Matysiak; Dorota Celinska-Kopczynska
data_source: UK Understanding Society (UKHLS) + text-mined climate news index
exposure_measure_content: Text-mined index of climate news coverage volume, linked to individual longitudinal records; moderated by pro-environmental intentions
exposure_items_quoted: a novel index of climate news coverage using text mining
notes: MEASURE-CONTENT FLAG: the exposure is media coverage volume, not expressed personal dread, so it is classed mixed rather than ecological_fear. The affective channel is restored only by the interaction with pro-environmental intentions, which is also where the whole effect sits — climate news coverage had no significant effect across political orientation. Preprint, no peer review.

title: The nexus between environmental concern and future childbearing aspirations among university students in Bangladesh
authors: Bijoya Saha; Shah Md Atiqul Haq
data_source: Structured questionnaire at Shahjalal University of Science and Technology
population: 380 final-year and masters students, one university
exposure_measure_content: Dichotomous single items on environmental concern, perceived vulnerability to extreme weather, and whether childlessness has a positive impact on the environment
exposure_items_quoted: a harmful environment can endanger the health of the child; childlessness has a positive impact on the environment
notes: THE ONLY NON-EUROPEAN/NON-US STUDY IN THE POOL — Bangladesh. Chapter sections 8 and 12 are wrong as written and must be corrected at TICK-053. DI classification is the weak form: two separately modelled DVs (intention yes/no, and intended count) rather than a design holding desire fixed. The only significant environmental predictor in the logistic model is the carbon-ethics item, which argues for PRIMARY_CARBON_ETHICS. Convenience sample, single university, dichotomous single-item measures.

authors: Sabrina Helm; Joya A. Kemper; Samantha White; David Dean
